Sample text:
---
At two in the morning, the freezing rain began to tick against the dome like handfuls of flung gravel. Arthur stood beneath the iron ribs of the Palm House, keeping his flashlight aimed at the wet herringbone brick so he wouldn’t disturb the finches tucked into the rafters. Outside, the city was disappearing beneath an iron-gray blizzard. Inside, it was seventy-four degrees and smelled of crushed peat, cinnamon bark, and stagnant rainwater.

He had worked the night shift at the municipal conservatory for eleven years. People often assumed the job was mostly security—checking latches, chasing off the occasional teenager hoping to smoke beneath a banana tree—but in winter, the job was almost entirely thermodynamics. Six hundred panes of Victorian glass were all that separated an acre of equatorial rainforest from a January gale. Every two hours, Arthur descended the concrete stairs beneath the Fern Gully to check the boilers, listening to the deep, rhythmic thrum of the burners and watching the brass pressure needles tremble near the red line. If the heat failed for even three hours on a night like this, a century of careful curation would turn to blackened pulp before sunrise.

He walked his circuit slowly, the soles of his boots squeaking on the damp stone. The conservatory was divided into four wings, each with its own climate and its own particular silence. The Arid House was the quietest; at night, the heat lamps clicked off and the room cooled to a crisp, desert chill. The agaves and barrel cacti stood in neat gravel beds like prehistoric sculptures, casting sharp, spiked shadows under the faint sodium glow leaking in from the streetlamps outside. 

From there, he passed through the heavy oak doors into the Orchidarium. The air immediately thickened, wrapping around his face like a warm cloth. Condensation gathered on the curved overhead struts and fell in unpredictable intervals—*plink* into a copper drainage trough, *thud* onto the broad, waxy leaf of a monstera. 

During the day, the conservatory belonged to spectacle. Schoolchildren pressed their noses against the koi pond; wedding parties posed beneath the wrought-iron arches; retirees murmured over the Latin plaques. Arthur had worked days once, years ago, and he hadn’t disliked it. Still, he preferred the hours after the last janitor locked the turnstiles. At night, the building stopped performing and simply breathed. Without voices echoing off the glass, you could hear the subtle mechanics of living things: the creak of a bamboo stalk shifting under its own weight, the papery rustle of a dried palm frond giving way, the soft, continuous hiss of the misting pipes.

A particularly fierce gust slammed against the western wall. High above him, the iron framework gave a low, metallic groan, and a shiver ran through the glass panes. Arthur paused, tipping his head back to scan the ceiling. A single cracked pane wouldn’t doom the room, not with the boilers running hard, but he checked anyway, tracing the beam of his flashlight along the putty seams. Everything held. There was something endlessly moving to him about the audacity of a greenhouse—the stubborn human insistence on building a fragile pocket of summer right in the teeth of the freeze.

He made his way back toward the central rotunda, where a sprawling, rather ungainly cactus hung from a rusted chain beside the eastern fountain. For nine months of the year, *Epiphyllum oxypetalum* looked like a tangle of flat green belts—the sort of plant visitors walked straight past on their way to the birds-of-paradise. But for the past week, Arthur had been watching a single reddish bud swell at the tip of one stem, curving upward like the neck of a swan.

Tonight, it was opening.

Arthur pulled an overturned terracotta pot close to the railing, switched off his flashlight, and sat down. As his eyes adjusted to the dim silver light filtering through the storm-streaked roof, the flower seemed to gather what little radiance existed in the room. Its outer sepals had peeled back, revealing dozens of thin, translucent white petals arranged in a starburst. At the center, a cluster of pale golden stamens trembled slightly in the draft from the floor vents.

A scent drifted toward him—cool, sweet, and faintly spicy, entirely different from the heavy rot and dampness of the surrounding soil. It smelled like rain on hot pavement, mixed with vanilla and something sharper he couldn’t quite name.

He sat with his hands resting on his knees and watched it unfold, millimeter by silent millimeter. He didn’t own a smartphone, and even if he had, he wouldn’t have taken a picture. There was a strange comfort in knowing that this particular bloom belonged to no one’s archive. The Queen of the Night opened only once, in the dark, and by the time the head botanist unlocked the front doors at eight o’clock, the petals would already be drooping, translucent edges curling inward toward decay. The morning visitors would see only a limp, spent husk dangling from an unattractive vine, never guessing what had happened in the dark while they slept.

The wind howled again, piling wet snow against the lower glass until the outside world vanished altogether into white static. Inside, the steam pipes knocked softly, faithful and steady. Arthur breathed in the vanishing perfume, feeling the warmth of the room settle deep into his coat, and stayed right where he was until the boiler timer chimed in his pocket, calling him back down to tend the fire.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A carefully composed literary scene centers on a night-shift conservatory worker witnessing a rare flower bloom during a storm.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and sensory, finding significance in close observation rather than dramatic action. Arthur’s quiet care—checking the boilers, avoiding disturbing the finches, and sitting with the flower instead of photographing it—gives the scene its pathos. The story invites the reader to attend to beauty that is brief, private, and likely to go unnoticed, while keeping that tenderness grounded in ordinary maintenance work.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds the conservatory as a fragile pocket of warmth amid winter, the largely unseen labor that keeps it alive, and the Queen of the Night’s fleeting bloom. It gives special weight to privacy and impermanence: the flower’s brief beauty matters even though it will not be recorded or seen by the morning visitors.

## Evidence line
> There was something endlessly moving to him about the audacity of a greenhouse—the stubborn human insistence on building a fragile pocket of summer right in the teeth of the freeze.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the scene is coherent and distinctive in its attention to quiet stewardship, sensory detail, and beauty that disappears without an audience.
